passage:
Monday, 11 am
Alka: Hi Jasleen, quick one. Pune client or Jaipur client first?
Jasleen: What are you leaning towards?
Alka: honestly no idea. just tell me and I'll do it 😅
Jasleen: I could. But I won't be on those calls, you will
Alka: I'm scared of picking wrong
Jasleen: Fair. Try this: two lines on why each one, then tell me what you'd choose
Alka: ok... Pune. bigger renewal and the contact already knows me
Jasleen: That's a solid reason. Go with it
Alka: wait, so you agree?
Jasleen: I agree that you HAVE a reason. Tell me on Friday how it went 🙂
Alka: ok. doing it

qa.q: Which client does Alka choose to start with?
qa.a: Alka chooses the Pune client.

qa.q: Why does Alka want Jasleen to just decide?
qa.a: Alka is scared of picking wrong and would like Jasleen to carry the decision.

qa.q: How does Jasleen help Alka build judgment rather than dependence?
qa.a: Jasleen asks Alka to write two lines of reasons, then choose, and asks for a report on Friday.

qa.q: Why might Jasleen refuse to simply give the answer?
qa.a: Jasleen will not be on the calls, so Alka needs the confidence to decide and to trust their own judgment.

grounding: A mentee keeps asking a mentor to decide for them out of fear of mistakes, and the mentor steers them toward making their own decision.

passage:
"He messaged me," Hansa said, turning the phone face down on the table. "Just 'hey, thought of you.'"

"Who, Neel?" Arohi asked.

"Yes. And now I'm remembering the Sunday mornings on the terrace, the tea, the old songs."

"Do you remember the Saturday nights when he didn't call?"

Hansa laughed, a little unwillingly. "Right. That too."

"What do you actually miss? Him, or being wanted?"

"Being wanted, maybe. And having someone to text at night."

"Then answer that question first, not him."

"I'll wait until tomorrow before I decide whether to reply."

"Text me if you want company tonight."

"I might."

qa.q: What did the message from the ex say?
qa.a: It said, "hey, thought of you."

qa.q: What does Hansa realise about what is being missed?
qa.a: Hansa suspects what is missed is the feeling of being wanted and having someone to text at night, more than Neel himself, which hints at loneliness.

qa.q: What could Hansa do before replying to Neel?
qa.a: Wait until tomorrow, think about what is missed and why it ended, and then decide whether to reply.

qa.q: Why does Arohi mention the Saturday nights when Neel didn't call?
qa.a: Arohi wants to balance the polished memories with the less happy ones, so Hansa sees the whole relationship.

grounding: An ex's message stirs longing and polished memories; the protagonist asks what is really missed and remembers why it ended before choosing.

passage: On the tram home from work in Melbourne, Noa's phone lit up with a photo from a mutual friend's party: Hiroshi, laughing, an arm around someone new. Noa's jaw tightened. It was not the photo itself; it was the memory of how Hiroshi had mocked Noa's interview nerves and then cancelled on Noa's birthday twice. Noa typed a long post full of dates and names, read it once, and did not send it. Instead Noa called Ellie, an old flatmate, and said, "I'm still furious and I hate that I am." Ellie said, "Of course you are. He treated you badly." By the last stop the draft was deleted, and Noa had booked a session with the counsellor that the college offered its alumni.

qa.q: Where was Noa when the photo appeared?
qa.a: Noa was on the tram home from work in Melbourne.

qa.q: Why did Noa say "I hate that I am"?
qa.a: Noa was angry about how Hiroshi had treated Noa and disliked still feeling it, since the anger keeps Noa tied to the past.

qa.q: What did Noa choose to do instead of sending the post?
qa.a: Noa called Ellie and booked a counsellor session, avoiding a revenge post.

qa.q: How might Ellie's reply have helped Noa?
qa.a: Ellie confirmed the anger was reasonable, so Noa did not need to feel ashamed of it.

grounding: The protagonist still feels angry at an ex, acknowledges the wrong, seeks support from a friend and a counsellor and avoids a revenge post.

passage:
Nandini: he came to my building again tonight
Sunaina: what? did he go up?
Nandini: security stopped him at the gate. he kept saying he only wanted to talk
Nandini: 14 calls today and messages since morning
Sunaina: have you answered any of them?
Nandini: I sent one last week. "It's over. Please don't contact me again." nothing since
Sunaina: good. don't reply to anything now
Nandini: I'm saving every screenshot and the call log
Sunaina: tell your parents tonight, and if he turns up again go to the police with the screenshots
Nandini: I'll tell Papa now
Sunaina: I'm coming over

qa.q: Who stopped Nandini's ex at the gate?
qa.a: Security stopped him at the gate.

qa.q: What does Nandini's saving of screenshots and the call log suggest Nandini is worried about?
qa.a: That the contact may continue or get worse, so a record will be needed for trusted people or the police.

qa.q: What has Nandini already done well, and what should follow?
qa.a: Nandini sent one clear final message and stopped replying; next come keeping records, telling family tonight and going to the police if he appears again.

qa.q: How does Sunaina react to the news?
qa.a: Sunaina is concerned and comes over at once.

grounding: An ex keeps calling and turning up after a clear no; the protagonist keeps one boundary, stops engaging, keeps records and tells trusted people.

passage:
Sunday. Sabina saw Bhupen's name in a friend's group photo and waited for the old sting. It did not come. Only tiredness. She carried that odd discovery around all week.

Saturday. Sabina sat with her notebook until late and wrote, "I forgive Bhupen. Not because he asked, he has not, but to put down what I have carried since 2019." It took the whole evening, and no reply was needed.

A month later. Bhupen wrote to say hello. Sabina answered kindly: "I hope you are well. I have made peace with how it ended, and I wish you well. I would rather not restart contact." She felt light, not triumphant.

qa.q: What did Sabina write in her notebook on Saturday?
qa.a: Sabina wrote that she forgave Bhupen, not because he asked, but to put down what she had carried since 2019.

qa.q: What does the missing sting on seeing the group photo suggest?
qa.a: The old hurt has faded enough for Sabina to feel ready to forgive.

qa.q: What made Sabina's reply to Bhupen a healthy way to close?
qa.a: It said she had made peace and wished him well, while clearly declining to restart contact.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt on receiving the reply?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt relieved or a little wistful, since the reply was kind but closed the door on contact.

grounding: Years later the protagonist forgives an ex for personal peace without needing an apology and without reopening the relationship.

passage: Sunday night. Sangeeta took three hours to reply to my text and I caught myself thinking, Dev would have called. Then I stopped. Dev did not call, most weeks. He sent long, beautiful messages on good days and vanished on the bad ones. I have kept the good days on a shelf in my head and thrown the rest away. Sangeeta, meanwhile, remembers my mother's birthday and turns up with soup when I am ill. That is a real person, not a highlight reel. What I actually want is a little more contact through the workday, and I have never said so. Tomorrow I will tell Sangeeta, calmly, that a quick afternoon check-in text would make me happy. Lakshmi

qa.q: Who remembers Lakshmi's mother's birthday?
qa.a: Sangeeta remembers it.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi stop the thought that Dev would have called?
qa.a: Lakshmi had felt impatient at the three-hour wait, then realised the memory was edited: Dev often vanished on bad days, so the comparison was unfair.

qa.q: What will Lakshmi say to Sangeeta tomorrow?
qa.a: That a quick afternoon check-in text would be welcome, said calmly.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel if Lakshmi never mentions this need?
qa.a: Sangeeta might not know anything is missing, since Lakshmi has never said so.

grounding: The protagonist compares a partner with an ex, sees the ex memory is edited, appreciates the partner and plans to state a need honestly.

passage:
Subject: Guess who was at Meenal's wedding

Dear Tara,

You asked how the wedding went, so here it is. I saw Yash near the dessert table with a plate in his hand and my stomach dropped. For about a second I considered pretending to read my phone. Then I walked over and said, "Hi, Yash. Good to see you. Congratulations on the new job." He said thanks, asked after my sister, and we talked for maybe two minutes. I did not put on a huge smile and I did not go cold either. Then I went back to the dance floor and my hands shook a little for ten minutes. It was not dramatic. I am glad I did not turn it into a show for the aunties.

Love,
Rashmi

qa.q: Where did Rashmi see Yash?
qa.a: Rashmi saw Yash near the dessert table at Meenal's wedding.

qa.q: What do Rashmi's shaking hands after the chat suggest?
qa.a: Rashmi was still anxious, even though the conversation went smoothly.

qa.q: How could Rashmi handle another chance meeting?
qa.a: Greet briefly and politely again and skip performing happiness or anger, as at the wedding.

qa.q: How might Yash have experienced the short chat?
qa.a: Yash probably found it civil and perhaps a relief, since Rashmi congratulated him and stayed brief.

grounding: The writer meets an ex at a friend's wedding, feels anxious, greets politely and briefly, and neither performs happiness nor anger.

passage: On Saturday morning a friend's story showed Nikita on a beach, laughing with someone I did not know. It hit me right under the ribs. My thumb hovered over her profile, wanting every tagged photo. Instead I put the phone in a drawer and went for a run. On the second lap I made myself say out loud why I had ended it: the months of cancelled plans, the way I had gone quiet to keep the peace. That helped more than I expected. By Sunday I had texted my cousin about the climbing trip I had been postponing for a year, and we picked a date. The stab came back once on Sunday night and left again. Gautam

qa.q: What did Gautam do instead of scrolling through Nikita's profile?
qa.a: Gautam put the phone in a drawer and went for a run.

qa.q: What did the stab under the ribs show about how Gautam felt?
qa.a: It showed jealousy at seeing Nikita happy with someone new, though Gautam still remembered the reasons for ending things.

qa.q: What small step helped Gautam turn attention to a life ahead?
qa.a: Texting the cousin and picking a date for the climbing trip that had been postponed.

qa.q: What would change if Gautam had kept scrolling through the tagged photos?
qa.a: The jealousy would probably grow and keep Gautam focused on Nikita rather than on plans of Gautam's own.

grounding: The protagonist feels a stab of jealousy at an ex's new happiness, lets it pass without stalking the profile and builds attention on life.

passage: "Her swim bag is by the door, and she has practice at five," Nkechi said. Hana answered, "Same as last week, then." Their voices stayed flat and short. For two years the handover had been the place for snapping about lateness, money, whose turn it was to go to the school fair. Nkechi felt the old heat rise at Hana's eye-roll about the bag, then looked at Ada, six years old, watching from the stairs with her shoes on the wrong feet. Nkechi swallowed the reply and said only, "Have a good weekend, both of you," then crouched to fix the shoes. Nkechi did not ask Ada to carry a message either. Hana's shoulders dropped an inch.

qa.q: How old is Ada?
qa.a: Ada is six years old.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi swallow the reply?
qa.a: Nkechi felt the old heat rise but put Ada's calm ahead of pride.

qa.q: How can Nkechi and Hana handle small disputes at handovers?
qa.a: Keep talks short and about Ada, settle bigger disagreements at another time, and never use Ada as a messenger.

qa.q: How might Ada experience the handover?
qa.a: Ada watches from the stairs with her shoes on the wrong feet, so she probably senses the tension and feels steadier when voices stay flat.

grounding: Two ex-partners who share a child keep the handover short, child-focused and respectful and do not use the child as a messenger.

passage: Sumit, you asked why I still call my mother every Sunday, though she once made me feel like a traitor for leaving. Sit; I will tell you. At twenty-four I got an offer from a firm two cities away. My mother stopped speaking to me for nine days, and I lay awake feeling like a traitor. Then came the headaches every time I mentioned it, and the line, "Go, go, if it finishes me, so be it." I nearly turned the offer down. What changed was a cousin saying, "Love could have said I will miss you." So I told my mother, gently, that I was going, that I would call every Sunday and come home for every festival. She sulked for a month, then began posting me pickles. The guilt lasted longer than the sulk. Mridul

qa.q: How many days did Mridul's mother stop speaking after the offer?
qa.a: She stopped speaking to Mridul for nine days.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling during the nine days of silence?
qa.a: Mridul felt guilty and torn, lying awake feeling like a traitor.

qa.q: How did Mridul set a boundary while keeping warmth?
qa.a: Mridul said gently that the move was happening and promised to call every Sunday and come home for every festival.

qa.q: How might the mother have seen the move?
qa.a: Her silence and talk of being finished suggest she feared being left alone, though it was not a fair way to say so.

grounding: An elder recalls a parent controlling through silence, headaches and guilt, and how gentle firm boundaries and warmth carried through.
